html:
The Battle of Amiens was fought from 8 to 12 August 1918 east of Amiens in northern France. Troops of the British Empire and France broke through the German lines on the first day and opened the advance that ended World War I.

After the Second Battle of the Marne the Allies held the initiative. The British commander Douglas Haig planned a surprise attack to free the railway through Amiens. British, Australian and Canadian troops and over 500 tanks were moved up in secret, at night. There was no long shelling to give warning. At dawn on 8 August, in fog, infantry, tanks, guns and aircraft attacked together. By evening they had gone about 11 km. Germany lost about 30,000 men that day, many of whom gave up without a fight. Ludendorff called it the black day of the German army.

Ludendorff told the emperor, Wilhelm II, that the war could no longer be won. The Allies attacked without pause for the next hundred days and broke the Hindenburg Line in September. Germany signed the armistice on 11 November 1918. Amiens became a model for attacks that combine tanks, infantry, artillery and aircraft.
